<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:intro-optimal}
Let $f=h+\overline g$ be an orientation-preserving harmonic mapping in $\mathbb D$ with $\left\lVert \omega_f\right\rVert_\infty<1$.  Then
\(
 K_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)
 =\inf_A K(A\circ f),
\)
where the infimum is over all orientation-preserving real-affine mappings of the target and $K(A\circ f)$ denotes the maximal differential eccentricity of $A\circ f$.  The infimum is attained.  The minimizing affine mappings are precisely those whose induced disk automorphism sends the unique hyperbolic circumcenter of $\overline{\omega_f(\mathbb D)}$ to the origin.  Any two minimizing affine mappings differ by an orientation-preserving Euclidean similarity.  If $f$ is globally univalent, the common minimum is the least quasiconformal constant among all orientation-preserving target-affine postcompositions of $f$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
Theorem \ref{thm:intro-optimal} provides an affine analogue of the classical extremal quasiconformal principle: minimizing the maximal differential eccentricity under target real-affine postcomposition is equivalent to placing the hyperbolic circumcenter of \(\omega_f(\mathbb D)\) at the origin, with uniqueness up to orientation-preserving Euclidean similarity. Unlike classical Teichm\"uller extremal theory, where extremality is governed by holomorphic quadratic differentials modulo M\"obius equivalence, our condition is formulated in terms of the hyperbolic geometry of the image of the complex dilatation. It yields an intrinsic canonical affine normalization for harmonic quasiconformal mappings.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:intro-support}
Let $f$ be as in Theorem \ref{thm:intro-optimal}, let $c=c_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)$ be the circumcenter of $\overline{\omega_f(\mathbb D)}$, and put $R=r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)$.  If $R>0$, there exist $m\in\{2,3\}$ and points
\(
 \xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m\in\overline{\omega_f(\mathbb D)}
\)
with $d_{\mathbb D}(c,\xi_j)=R$ such that $c$ is already the circumcenter of $\{\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m\}$.  If $m=2$, then $c$ is the hyperbolic midpoint of $\xi_1$ and $\xi_2$.  If $m=3$, the outward unit tangent vectors at $c$ toward the $\xi_j$ have the origin in their Euclidean convex hull in $T_c\mathbb D$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:intro-jung}
For every orientation-preserving harmonic mapping $f$ in $\mathbb D$ with $\left\lVert \omega_f\right\rVert_\infty<1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-jung}
 \frac{d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)}{2}
 \le r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)
 \le
 J\bigl(d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)\bigr),
 \quad
 J(t)=\operatorname{arcsinh}\!\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\sinh\frac t2\right).
\end{equation}
Both inequalities are sharp within the class of globally univalent harmonic quasiconformal mappings.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:intro-ps}
Let $f$ be an orientation-preserving harmonic mapping in $\mathbb D$ with $\left\lVert \omega_f\right\rVert_\infty<1$, and let
\(
 F=\mathscr B[f]=H+\overline G
\)
be the canonical balanced representative defined in Section \ref{sec:canonical}.  Put
\[
 k=\left\lVert G'/H'\right\rVert_\infty=k_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)<1.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-ps}
 \left\lVert P_H-P_f\right\rVert
 =\left\lVert P_H-P_F\right\rVert
 \le \mathcal C(k),
\end{equation}
where, for $0<k<1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Ck-intro}
\mathcal C(k)
 =\frac{\sqrt{x_k}(k^2-x_k)}{k(1-x_k)}
 =\frac{2x_k^{3/2}}{k(1+x_k)},
 \end{equation}
in which $x_k\in(0,1)$ is the unique solution to
\[
\frac{\sqrt{x}(k^2-x)}{k(1-x)}=\frac{2x^{3/2}}{k(1+x)},
\]
given by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:xk-intro}
 x_k=\frac{3-k^2-\sqrt{(1-k^2)(9-k^2)}}{2},
\end{equation}
and $\mathcal C(0)=0$.  The estimate is sharp for every $0<k<1$.  Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Ck-asymptotic-intro}
 \mathcal C(k)=\frac{2}{3\sqrt3}k^2+O(k^4)
 \quad(k\to0).
\end{equation}
For any orientation-preserving target-affine mapping $A$, the same universal estimate holds with the parameter $\left\lVert \omega_{A\circ f}\right\rVert_\infty$ in place of $k$, and balancing minimizes this parameter over the affine orbit.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:affine-aut}
For every $A$ as in \eqref{eq:A-def}, the mapping
\begin{equation}\label{eq:T-A}
 T_A(\zeta)=\frac{\overline a\,\zeta+\overline b}{b\,\zeta+a}
\end{equation}
is an automorphism of $\mathbb D$.  Conversely, every automorphism of $\mathbb D$ is $T_A$ for some orientation-preserving real-affine $A$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Write $q=b/a$, so $|q|<1$.  Then
\[
 T_A(\zeta)
 =\frac{\overline a}{a}\cdot
 \frac{\zeta+\overline q}{1+q\,\zeta},
\]
which is a disk automorphism.  Conversely, every $T\in\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb D)$ has the form
\[
 T(\zeta)=e^{i\theta}\frac{\zeta-c}{1-\overline c\,\zeta}.
\]
Take $q=-\overline c$, choose $a$ with $\overline a/a=e^{i\theta}$, and set $b=aq$.  Then $|b|<|a|$ and $T=T_A$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:rad-basic}
Let $E\subset\mathbb D$ be nonempty and hyperbolically bounded, with circumradius $R$ and circumcenter $c$.  Then
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $\operatorname{diam}_{\mathbb D}(E)\le2R$;
\item if $T\in\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb D)$, then
$\operatorname{rad}_{\mathbb D}(T(E))=R$,
$\operatorname{diam}_{\mathbb D}(T(E))=\operatorname{diam}_{\mathbb D}(E)$,
and the circumcenter of $T(E)$ is $T(c)$;
\item $\operatorname{rad}_{\mathbb D}(E)=\operatorname{rad}_{\mathbb D}(\overline E)$ and
$\operatorname{diam}_{\mathbb D}(E)=\operatorname{diam}_{\mathbb D}(\overline E)$;
\item $\operatorname{rad}_{\mathbb D}(E)=\operatorname{rad}_{\mathbb D}(\operatorname{hconv}E)$, where $\operatorname{hconv}$ denotes the hyperbolic geodesic convex hull.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Part (i) follows from the triangle inequality.  Part (ii) follows from isometric invariance and uniqueness of the circumcenter.  Part (iii) follows by continuity of the distance.  Finally, hyperbolic balls are geodesically convex.  Hence every ball containing $E$ contains $\operatorname{hconv}E$, while the reverse inequality for circumradii is immediate from inclusion.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:diam-convex-hull}
For every bounded $E\subset\mathbb D$, we have
\(
 \operatorname{diam}_{\mathbb D}(\operatorname{hconv}E)=\operatorname{diam}_{\mathbb D}(E).
\)
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
In a CAT$(0)$ space, the distance between points moving proportionally on two geodesic segments is a convex function of the parameter. Therefore, the diameter does not increase when one replaces either endpoint by a point on a geodesic segment joining two old points.  Iterating this observation over finite geodesic hulls and then taking closures proves the claim.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:aff-invariants}
Let $f=h+\overline g$ be orientation-preserving in $\mathbb D$ and suppose that $\omega_f(\mathbb D)$ is hyperbolically bounded.  Set
\(
 E_f=\overline{\omega_f(\mathbb D)}.
\)
The \emph{affine circumcenter}, \emph{affine radius}, and \emph{affine diameter} of $f$ are
\begin{align}
 c_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)&= {\rm{c}}_{\rm{hyp}}(E_f),\label{eq:cA}\\
 r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)&=\operatorname{rad}_{\mathbb D}(E_f),\label{eq:rA}\\
 d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)&=\operatorname{diam}_{\mathbb D}(E_f).
\end{align}

We also define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kA-KA}
 k_{\mathrm{aff}}(f):=\tanh\frac{r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)}2,
 \quad
 K_{\mathrm{aff}}(f):=\frac{1+k_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)}{1-k_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)}=e^{r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)},
\end{equation}
and the \emph{pseudohyperbolic affine oscillation} is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:qA}
 q_{\mathrm{aff}}(f):=\tanh\frac{d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)}2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:full-invariance}
Let $f$ be as in Definition \ref{def:aff-invariants}. 
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item If $A$ is any orientation-preserving real-affine mapping of the target, then
\[
 r_{\mathrm{aff}}(A\circ f)=r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f),\ \
 d_{\mathrm{aff}}(A\circ f)=d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f),\ \
 K_{\mathrm{aff}}(A\circ f)=K_{\mathrm{aff}}(f),\ \
 q_{\mathrm{aff}}(A\circ f)=q_{\mathrm{aff}}(f).
\]
Moreover,
\[
 c_{\mathrm{aff}}(A\circ f)=T_A(c_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)).
\]
\item If $\phi\in\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb D)$, then
\[
 r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f\circ\phi)=r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f),\quad
 d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f\circ\phi)=d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f).
\]
The same holds for normalized harmonic Koebe transforms.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
By \eqref{eq:omega-transform}, we have
\(
 E_{A\circ f}=T_A(E_f),
\)
and $T_A$ is a hyperbolic isometry by Lemma \ref{lem:affine-aut}.  Part (i) now follows from Lemma \ref{lem:rad-basic}.  By \eqref{eq:precomp-omega}, precomposition by a disk automorphism does not change the dilatation image as a set.  A target similarity, used in the usual normalization of a Koebe transform, rotates the dilatation image, hence preserves all the listed quantities.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:zero-defect}
For an orientation-preserving harmonic mapping $f=h+\overline g$ in $\mathbb D$, the following statements are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)=0$;
\item $r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)=0$;
\item $\omega_f$ is constant;
\item there exists an orientation-preserving real-affine mapping $A$ such that $A\circ f$ is analytic.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The equivalence of (i)-(iii) is immediate.  Suppose $\omega_f\equiv\lambda$ with $|\lambda|<1$.  Then $g'=\lambda h'$, i.e., $g=\lambda h+C$.  Hence
\[
 f=h+\overline\lambda\,\overline h+\overline C.
\]
For
\[
 A(w)=w-\overline\lambda\,\overline w,
\]
we obtain
\[
 A\circ f=(1-|\lambda|^2)h+C-\lambda\overline{C},
\]
which is analytic.  Conversely, if $A\circ f$ is analytic, then $\omega_{A\circ f}\equiv0$.  Since \(\omega_{A\circ f}=T_A\circ\omega_f\) and $T_A$ is injective, $\omega_f$ is constant.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
The usual number $k(f)=\left\lVert \omega_f\right\rVert_\infty$ measures the distance of the dilatation range from the distinguished origin of the disk model.  By contrast, $r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)$ measures the radius of the smallest hyperbolic disk containing the range, with the center allowed to move.  Thus $r_{\mathrm{aff}}$ removes precisely the non-intrinsic choice introduced by the target affine gauge.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:bounded-iff-qc}
For an orientation-preserving harmonic mapping $f$ in $\mathbb D$, the following statements are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $\left\lVert \omega_f\right\rVert_\infty<1$;
\item $r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)<\infty$;
\item $d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)<\infty$;
\item $q_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)<1$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
If $\left\lVert \omega_f\right\rVert_\infty\le k<1$, then $E_f$ lies in the compact Euclidean disk $|\zeta|\le k$, hence has finite hyperbolic diameter and radius. Since $d_{\mathrm{aff}}\le2r_{\mathrm{aff}}$ always holds, (ii) implies (iii).  Conversely, if $E_f$ has finite hyperbolic diameter, choose $\zeta_0\in E_f$.  Then
\(
 E_f\subset \overline B_{\mathbb D}(\zeta_0,d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)),
\)
which is compactly contained in $\mathbb D$, proving (i).  Finally, (iii) and (iv) are equivalent by \eqref{eq:qA}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
An orientation-preserving harmonic mapping $f$ with uniformly bounded differential distortion is called \emph{affine-balanced}, or simply \emph{balanced}, if
\(
 c_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)=0.
\)
Equivalently, the smallest hyperbolic disk containing $E_f$ is centered at $0$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:optimal}
Let $f$ be an orientation-preserving harmonic mapping in $\mathbb D$ with $\left\lVert \omega_f\right\rVert_\infty<1$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:optimal-main}
 \logK_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)
 =r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)
 =\inf_A\log K(A\circ f),
\end{equation}
where $A$ ranges over all orientation-preserving target-affine mappings.  The infimum is attained.

Let $c=c_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)$.  An affine mapping $A$ is minimizing if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:min-characterization}
 T_A(c)=0.
\end{equation}
Any two minimizing affine mappings differ by an orientation-preserving Euclidean similarity.  In particular, the balanced representative is unique up to similarity.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
By \eqref{eq:omega-transform}, \eqref{eq:logK-hyp},  and hyperbolic invariance, we obtain
\begin{align*}
 \log K(A\circ f)
 =\sup_{\zeta\in E_f}d_{\mathbb D}(0,T_A(\zeta))
 =\sup_{\zeta\in E_f}d_{\mathbb D}(T_A^{-1}(0),\zeta)
 =r_{E_f}(T_A^{-1}(0)).
\end{align*}
By Lemma \ref{lem:affine-aut}, as $A$ varies, $T_A^{-1}(0)$ ranges over all of $\mathbb D$.  Therefore,
\[
 \inf_A\log K(A\circ f)
 =\inf_{p\in\mathbb D}r_{E_f}(p)
 =r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f).
\]
Since $E_f$ is hyperbolically bounded, it has a unique circumcenter $c$.  Hence the minimum is attained exactly when $T_A^{-1}(0)=c$, equivalently, $T_A(c)=0$.

If $A_1$ and $A_2$ are both minimizing, set $C=A_2\circ A_1^{-1}$.  By the composition rule for the induced disk automorphisms, we have
\(
 T_C=T_{A_2}\circ T_{A_1}^{-1},
\)
and this automorphism fixes $0$.  Hence it is a rotation.  If $C(w)=\alpha w+\beta\overline w+\gamma$, then $T_C(0)=\overline\beta/\alpha=0$, so $\beta=0$.  Therefore, $C(w)=\alpha w+\gamma$ is an orientation-preserving Euclidean similarity.  Thus the minimizing gauge is unique modulo such similarities.

Finally, exponentiating
\[
 \inf_A\log K(A\circ f)=r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)
\]
gives
\[
 \inf_A K(A\circ f)=e^{r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)}=K_{\mathrm{aff}}(f),
\]
which is the identity stated in Theorem \ref{thm:intro-optimal}.  If $f$ is globally univalent, every orientation-preserving affine postcomposition remains a homeomorphism onto its image, so this maximal differential distortion is precisely the quasiconformal constant.  The final assertion of Theorem \ref{thm:intro-optimal} follows.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
Consider the mapping \begin{equation}\label{63}
 f_k(z)=z+\frac{k}{2}\overline{z}^2\quad({0<k<1}).
\end{equation} Here \(\omega_{f_k}(\mathbb D)=k\mathbb D\), whose hyperbolic circumcenter is the origin. The identity mapping is already a minimizer, so \[K_{\text{aff}}(f_k)=K(f_k)=\frac{1+k}{1-k}.\] Any nontrivial target-affine postcomposition increases the maximal differential eccentricity. Since \(f_k\) is globally univalent, \(K_{\text{aff}}(f_k)\) is indeed the minimal quasiconformal constant within the family \(\{A\circ f_k\}\).
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
Choose \[\omega(z)=k\,\frac{z+a}{1+\overline{a}z}\] with \(0<k<1\) and \(0<|a|<1\), a rotated Blaschke factor. The mapping \[f(z)=z+\overline{\int_0^z\omega(\zeta)\,d\zeta}\] is globally univalent. The image set \(\omega_f(\mathbb D)\) is a disk whose hyperbolic circumcenter is displaced away from the origin. The identity mapping is not a minimizer. Theorem~\ref{thm:intro-optimal} guarantees an optimal real-affine postcomposition \(A^*\), shifting the hyperbolic circumcenter to zero, which yields the minimal value \(K_{\text{aff}}(f)=K(A^*\circ f)\). This illustrates that target‑affine normalization can strictly reduce the maximal differential eccentricity of a harmonic mapping.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:balanced-k}
If $f$ is balanced, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:balanced-k}
 \left\lVert \omega_f\right\rVert_\infty=k_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)
 =\tanh\frac{r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)}2,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:balanced-K}
 K(f)=K_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)=e^{r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)}.
\end{equation}
For an arbitrary affine representative $F=A\circ f$,
\(
 K(F)\geK_{\mathrm{aff}}(f).
\)
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
If the circumcenter is $0$, then
\[
 r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)=\sup_{\zeta\in E_f}d_{\mathbb D}(0,\zeta)
 =2\operatorname{arctanh}\left\lVert \omega_f\right\rVert_\infty.
\]
The formulas follow.  The last assertion is Theorem~\ref{thm:optimal}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:center-equiv}
For every orientation-preserving real-affine mapping $A$, we have
\(
 c_{\mathrm{aff}}(A\circ f)=T_A(c_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)).
\)
Consequently, the assignment $f\mapstoc_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)$ is not invariant but is equivariant, while $r_{\mathrm{aff}}$, $d_{\mathrm{aff}}$, $K_{\mathrm{aff}}$, and $q_{\mathrm{aff}}$ are invariant.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
This is Proposition \ref{prop:full-invariance}, but it is worth isolating because it shows that the center itself carries the exact affine covariance needed to define a canonical gauge.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:contact-balance}
With the notation above,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:contact-hull}
 0\in\operatorname{conv}\{u_\zeta:\zeta\in\Gamma(E)\}
 \subset T_c\mathbb D\cong\mathbb R^2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Suppose not.  Since the convex hull is compact and does not contain $0$, the strict separation theorem gives a unit vector $v\in T_c\mathbb D$ and $\eta>0$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:strict-sep}
 \left\langle u_\zeta,v\right\rangle\ge\eta
 \quad(\zeta\in\Gamma(E)).
\end{equation}
Let $c_t=\exp_c(tv)$ for small $t\ge0$ and put
\(
 F(t,\zeta)=d_{\mathbb D}(c_t,\zeta).
\)
Since $R>0$, the compact contact set is separated from $c$.  Thus $F$ is smooth in the first variable on a neighborhood of $\{0\}\times\Gamma(E)$, and the first variation formula gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:first-var}
 \partial_tF(0,\zeta)
 =-\left\langle u_\zeta,v\right\rangle
 \le-\eta
 \quad(\zeta\in\Gamma(E)).
\end{equation}
By compactness and continuity of $\partial_tF$, there exists a relative neighborhood $U$ of $\Gamma(E)$ in $E$ and $\tau>0$ such that
\[
 \partial_tF(t,\zeta)\le-\frac{\eta}{2}
 \quad(0\le t\le\tau,\ \zeta\in U).
\]
Consequently,
\[
 F(t,\zeta)\le F(0,\zeta)-\frac{\eta t}{2}
 \le R-\frac{\eta t}{2}
 \quad(0<t\le\tau,\ \zeta\in U).
\]
On the compact complement $E\setminus U$, one has
\(
 \max_{\zeta\in E\setminus U}F(0,\zeta)=R-\varepsilon
\)
for some $\varepsilon>0$.  Uniform continuity of $F$ on a compact parameter interval then implies, after decreasing $t>0$ if necessary,
\[
 F(t,\zeta)\le R-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
 \quad(\zeta\in E\setminus U).
\]
Thus \(\sup_{\zeta\in E}F(t,\zeta)<R,\) contradicting the minimality of $c$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:support}
Let $E\subset\mathbb D$ be nonempty and compact, with circumcenter $c$ and radius $R>0$.  Then there exist $m\in\{2,3\}$ and contact points $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m\in\Gamma(E)$ such that $c$ is the circumcenter of $\{\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m\}$.
More precisely:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item if $m=2$, then the tangent directions $u_{\xi_1}$ and $u_{\xi_2}$ are opposite, so $c$ is the midpoint of the geodesic segment $[\xi_1,\xi_2]$ and
\(
 d_{\mathbb D}(\xi_1,\xi_2)=2R;
\)
\item if $m=3$, then there are positive numbers $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$ with $\lambda_1+\lambda_2+\lambda_3=1$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:three-balance}
 \lambda_1u_{\xi_1}+\lambda_2u_{\xi_2}+\lambda_3u_{\xi_3}=0.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{lem:contact-balance}, $0$ lies in the convex hull of the contact directions.  Carath\'eodory's theorem for convex hulls~\cite[Theorem 17.1]{Rockafellar1970} in the two-dimensional vector space $T_c\mathbb D$ shows that $0$ lies in the convex hull of at most three such vectors.  One vector cannot suffice, so $m\in\{2,3\}$ after removing redundancy.

If $m=2$, two unit vectors have $0$ in their segment only when they are opposite.  Thus the corresponding geodesics form one geodesic through $c$, with equal endpoint distance $R$.  Hence $c$ is their midpoint.

If $m=3$ and no two already suffice, then $0$ lies in the interior of the Euclidean triangle spanned by the three unit vectors.  This gives strictly positive barycentric coefficients satisfying \eqref{eq:three-balance}.

It remains to see that $c$ is the circumcenter of the selected points.  If a ball of radius $R'<R$ contained them, let $p$ be its center.  In the two-point case, this contradicts $d(\xi_1,\xi_2)=2R$.  Assume therefore that $m=3$, put $L=d_{\mathbb D}(c,p)>0$ and let $\gamma:[0,L]\to\mathbb D$ be the unit-speed geodesic from $c$ to $p$, with $v=\gamma'(0)$.  For each $j$, the function
\(
 t\longmapsto d_{\mathbb D}(\gamma(t),\xi_j)
\)
is convex, because $\mathbb D$ is CAT$(0)$.  Its value at $t=L$ is strictly smaller than its value $R$ at $t=0$, so convexity implies that its right derivative at $0$ is negative.  By the first variation formula, this gives
\[
 \left\langle u_{\xi_j},v\right\rangle>0
 \quad(j=1,2,3).
\]
Multiplying by the positive coefficients in \eqref{eq:three-balance} and summing yields
\[
 0=\left\langle \lambda_1u_{\xi_1}+\lambda_2u_{\xi_2}+\lambda_3u_{\xi_3},v\right\rangle>0,
\]
which is a contradiction.  Thus the selected finite set has circumradius $R$ and circumcenter $c$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Set
\[
 E=E_f=\overline{\omega_f(\mathbb D)},\quad
 c=c_{\mathrm{aff}}(f),\quad R=r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)>0,
\]
and let
\[
 \Gamma=\{\zeta\in E:d_{\mathbb D}(c,\zeta)=R\}
\]
be the contact set.  It is nonempty and compact.  For $\zeta\in\Gamma$, let $u_\zeta$ be the unit tangent at $c$ pointing toward $\zeta$.

We first prove the balancing relation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-contact-balance}
 0\in\operatorname{conv}\{u_\zeta:\zeta\in\Gamma\}.
\end{equation}
If this were false, strict separation in the Euclidean plane $T_c\mathbb D$ would give a unit vector $v$ and $\eta>0$ such that
\[
 \langle u_\zeta,v\rangle\ge\eta
 \quad(\zeta\in\Gamma).
\]
Put $c_t=\exp_c(tv)$.  The first variation formula gives
\[
 \left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}d_{\mathbb D}(c_t,\zeta)
 =-\langle u_\zeta,v\rangle\le-\eta
 \quad(\zeta\in\Gamma).
\]
Because $R>0$, the contact set stays away from $c$.  Compactness and continuity of the first derivative therefore give a neighborhood $U$ of $\Gamma$ and $t_0>0$ such that, for $0<t<t_0$ and $\zeta\in E\cap U$,
\[
 d_{\mathbb D}(c_t,\zeta)\le d_{\mathbb D}(c,\zeta)-\frac{\eta}{2}t
 \le R-\frac{\eta}{2}t.
\]
On the compact complement $E\setminus U$, there is an $\varepsilon>0$ with
\[
 d_{\mathbb D}(c,\zeta)\le R-\varepsilon.
\]
Since $d_{\mathbb D}(c,c_t)=t$, the triangle inequality gives, after decreasing $t_0$ if necessary,
\[
 d_{\mathbb D}(c_t,\zeta)\le R-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
 \quad(\zeta\in E\setminus U,\ 0<t<t_0).
\]
Thus \[\sup_{\zeta\in E}d_{\mathbb D}(c_t,\zeta)<R,\] contradicting the defining minimality of the circumcenter.  This proves \eqref{eq:intro-contact-balance}.

Carath\'eodory's theorem in the two-dimensional vector space $T_c\mathbb D$ now yields contact points $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m$ with $m\le3$ whose tangent directions already have $0$ in their convex hull.  Since each $u_{\xi_j}$ is a unit vector, one point cannot suffice; hence $m\in\{2,3\}$.

If $m=2$, the two unit vectors must be opposite.  The geodesics from $c$ to $\xi_1$ and $\xi_2$ therefore form one geodesic, and both endpoints are at distance $R$ from $c$.  Hence $c$ is the hyperbolic midpoint and
\(
 d_{\mathbb D}(\xi_1,\xi_2)=2R.
\)

Assume $m=3$ and no pair suffices.  Then $0$ lies in the interior of the Euclidean triangle spanned by the three unit directions, so there are $\lambda_j>0$ with $\lambda_1+\lambda_2+\lambda_3=1$ and
\[
 \lambda_1u_{\xi_1}+\lambda_2u_{\xi_2}+\lambda_3u_{\xi_3}=0.
\]
It remains only to check that $c$ is the circumcenter of these selected points.  Suppose instead that some $p$ satisfies
\[
 d_{\mathbb D}(p,\xi_j)<R\quad(j=1,2,3).
\]
Let $\gamma:[0,L]\to\mathbb D$ be the unit-speed geodesic from $c$ to $p$, where $L=d_{\mathbb D}(c,p)>0$, and let $v=\gamma\,'(0)$.  Since the hyperbolic disk is CAT$(0)$, each function
\[
 t\longmapsto d_{\mathbb D}(\gamma(t),\xi_j)
\]
is convex.  Its value at $L$ is strictly smaller than its value $R$ at $0$, so its right derivative at $0$ is negative.  By first variation, we obtain
\(
 \langle u_{\xi_j},v\rangle>0.
\)
Multiplying by $\lambda_j$ and summing gives
\[
 0=\left\langle\lambda_1u_{\xi_1}+\lambda_2u_{\xi_2}+\lambda_3u_{\xi_3},v\right\rangle>0,
\]
a contradiction.  Thus $c$ is the circumcenter of the selected two or three contact points, and all assertions of Theorem~\ref{thm:intro-support} follow.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
Let \(\omega:\mathbb D\to\mathbb D\) be analytic such that \(\omega(\mathbb D)\) is a hyperbolic line segment with endpoints \(\xi_1,\xi_2\). Its hyperbolic circumcenter \(c\) is the hyperbolic midpoint of \(\xi_1\) and \(\xi_2\), and the hyperbolic circumradius equals \(d_{\mathbb D}(c,\xi_1)=d_{\mathbb D}(c,\xi_2)\). Only two extreme points are needed to determine \(c\), so \(m=2\). This realizes the two-point case of Theorem~\ref{thm:intro-support}. The mapping \[f(z)=z+\overline{\int_0^z\omega(\zeta)\,d\zeta}\] constructed via our realization lemma gives a concrete globally univalent harmonic mapping for this configuration.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
Choose a scaled third‑order Blaschke product \(\omega\), such that \(\omega(\mathbb D)\) is a compact subset of \(\mathbb D\) whose hyperbolic circumcenter \(c\) cannot be determined by only two boundary points. There exist three points \(\xi_1,\xi_2,\xi_3\in\omega(\mathbb D)\) with \(d_{\mathbb D}(c,\xi_j)=R\). The outward unit tangent vectors at \(c\) toward each \(\xi_j\) have the origin inside their Euclidean convex hull within \(T_c\mathbb D\). This configuration realizes the three-point case of Theorem~\ref{thm:intro-support}. Again our realization lemma yields an explicit globally univalent harmonic mapping associated with this dilatation set.
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:affine-jung}
For every orientation-preserving harmonic mapping $f$ with $\left\lVert \omega_f\right\rVert_\infty<1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:affine-jung}
 \frac{d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)}2
 \le r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)
 \le J(d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)).
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:KA-jung}
 \exp\left(\frac{d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)}{2}\right)
 \le K_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)
 \le \exp(J(d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f))).
\end{equation}
Both bounds are sharp among globally univalent harmonic quasiconformal mappings.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The lower bound follows from $d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)\le2r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:rad-basic}.  The upper bound is Dekster's theorem applied to $E_f$.  Since $K_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)=e^{r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)}$, exponentiation gives \eqref{eq:KA-jung}.  This proves the inequality part of Theorem~\ref{thm:intro-jung}; the two sharpness constructions are given in Section~\ref{sec:examples}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:pseudohyp-jung}
Let $q=q_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)\in[0,1)$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kA-lower-q}
 k_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)\ge \frac{q}{1+\sqrt{1-q^2}}
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kA-upper-q}
 k_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)
 \le
 j(q):=
 \frac{2q}
 {\sqrt{3+q^2}+\sqrt{3(1-q^2)}}.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:KA-q}
 \sqrt{\frac{1+q}{1-q}}
 \le K_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)
 \le \frac{1+j(q)}{1-j(q)}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The lower bound follows from
\[
 k_{\mathrm{aff}}=\tanh\frac{r_{\mathrm{aff}}}{2}
 \ge\tanh\frac{d_{\mathrm{aff}}}{4}
 =\tanh\left(\frac12\operatorname{arctanh} q\right)
 =\frac{q}{1+\sqrt{1-q^2}}.
\]
For the upper bound, set
\[
 X=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\sinh\frac{d_{\mathrm{aff}}}{2}
 =\frac{2q}{\sqrt3\sqrt{1-q^2}}.
\]
Then
\[
 k_{\mathrm{aff}}\le\tanh\left(\frac12\operatorname{arcsinh} X\right)
 =\frac{X}{1+\sqrt{1+X^2}},
\]
which simplifies to \eqref{eq:kA-upper-q}.  The statement for $K_{\mathrm{aff}}$ follows from 
\[K_{\mathrm{aff}}=\frac{1+k_{\mathrm{aff}}}{1-k_{\mathrm{aff}}}.\]
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:small-jung}
As $D\to0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:J-small}
 J(D)=\frac{D}{\sqrt3}+O(D^3).
\end{equation}
Then
\[
 \frac D2\ler_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)\le\frac D{\sqrt3}+O(D^3)
 \ \text{when }d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)=D\to0.
\]
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Using \[\sinh\frac D2=\frac D2+O(D^3)\] and \[\operatorname{arcsinh} x=x+O(x^3),\] we get the desired asymptotic expansion.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:realization}
Let $\omega:\mathbb D\to\mathbb D$ be analytic and suppose $\left\lVert \omega\right\rVert_\infty\le k<1$.  Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:realization-f}
 g(z)=\int_0^z\omega(\zeta)\,d\zeta,
 \quad
 f(z)=z+\overline{g(z)}.
\end{equation}
Then $f$ is orientation-preserving, globally univalent, and $K$-quasiconformal with
\[
 K\le\frac{1+k}{1-k}.
\]
Its second dilatation is exactly $\omega$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Note that $h(z)=z$ and $g'(z)=\omega(z)$. The second dilatation is $\omega$ and $J_f=1-|\omega|^2>0$.  Since the unit disk is convex, for $z,w\in\mathbb D$, the line segment joining them lies in $\mathbb D$, and
\[
 |g(z)-g(w)|
 \le k|z-w|.
\]
Therefore,
\[
 |f(z)-f(w)|
 \ge |z-w|-|g(z)-g(w)|
 \ge(1-k)|z-w|.
\]
Thus $f$ is injective and co-Lipschitz.  The quasiconformal bound follows from \eqref{eq:pointwise-K}.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The sharpness construction uses only two classical ingredients: the Riemann mapping theorem and the realization lemma.  It shows that no holomorphic constraint on the dilatation improves the universal hyperbolic Jung constant.  Although $\omega(\mathbb D)$ is open when $\omega$ is nonconstant, the interior of an equilateral hyperbolic  triangle is already an open extremal domain.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Let $E_f=\overline{\omega_f(\mathbb D)}$, $R=r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)$, and $D=d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)$.  If $c$ is the circumcenter of $E_f$, then for any $\zeta,\eta\in E_f$, we have
\[
 d_{\mathbb D}(\zeta,\eta)\le d_{\mathbb D}(\zeta,c)+d_{\mathbb D}(c,\eta)\le 2R.
\]
Taking the supremum gives $D/2\le R$.  The upper estimate
\[
 R\le J(D)=\operatorname{arcsinh}\!\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\sinh\frac D2\right)
\]
is exactly the two-dimensional curvature $-1$ case of Dekster's sharp hyperbolic Jung theorem~\cite{Dekster1995}; see also \cite[Theorem 3.3]{NasserRainioVuorinen2022}.

It remains to verify sharpness within the harmonic univalent category.  For the lower bound, given $0<k<1$, Take $\omega(z)=kz$ and realize it via Lemma~\ref{lem:realization}, yielding the mapping $f_k$ given by \eqref{63}.
Then $E_{f_k}=\{\lvert\zeta\rvert\le k\}$ is the hyperbolic disk centered at $0$ of radius $2\operatorname{arctanh} k$, so
\[
 r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f_k)=2\operatorname{arctanh} k,\quad d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f_k)=4\operatorname{arctanh} k=2r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f_k).
\]
Because $4\operatorname{arctanh} k$ ranges over $(0,\infty)$, equality in the lower bound occurs for every prescribed positive affine diameter.

For the upper bound, fix $D>0$ and let $\Omega_D$ be the interior of a regular equilateral hyperbolic triangle of side length $D$, chosen with compact closure in $\mathbb D$.  Its circumradius is $J(D)$.  Let $\omega_D:\mathbb D\to\Omega_D$ be a Riemann mapping and realize $\omega_D$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:realization}.  Since $\overline{\Omega_D}\Subset\mathbb D$, the resulting mapping is globally univalent harmonic quasiconformal, and
\[
 d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)=D,\quad r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)=J(D).
\]
Thus the upper bound is also attained for every $D>0$.  This proves both inequalities and both sharpness assertions.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- example-5: body_md -->
Choose an analytic mapping \(\omega\colon\mathbb D\to\mathbb D\) such that \(\omega(\mathbb D)\) is a hyperbolic line segment with endpoints \(\xi_1,\xi_2\). The hyperbolic diameter is \(d(f)=d_{\mathbb D}(\xi_1,\xi_2)\). The hyperbolic circumcenter \(c\) is the hyperbolic midpoint of \(\xi_1\) and \(\xi_2\), so that \(r(f)=d(f)/2\). Hence the lower bound in \eqref{eq:intro-jung} is attained. Our realization lemma produces a globally univalent harmonic quasiconformal mapping \[f(z)=z+\overline{\int_0^z\omega(\zeta)\,d\zeta}\] for this configuration.
<!-- end example-5 -->
<!-- example-6: body_md -->
Let \(\omega\) be a suitably scaled third-order Blaschke product such that the hyperbolic convex hull of \(\omega(\mathbb D)\) is an equilateral hyperbolic triangle with vertices \(\xi_1,\xi_2,\xi_3\). All three vertices lie on a common hyperbolic circle centered at \(c\), the hyperbolic circumcenter of the set. The pairwise hyperbolic distances between vertices are equal to \(d(f)\), and the circumradius satisfies \(r(f)=J(d(f))\). The outward unit tangent vectors at \(c\) toward the three vertices contain the origin in their convex hull in \(T_c\mathbb D\), consistent with the three-point support principle. The mapping constructed via the realization lemma is globally univalent and attains the upper bound in \eqref{eq:intro-jung}.
<!-- end example-6 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:omega0-comparison}
Suppose $f$ is an orientation-preserving harmonic mapping with $\left\lVert \omega_f\right\rVert_\infty<1$ and
\(
 \omega_f(0)=0.
\)
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sqrtK}
 \sqrt{K(f)}\leK_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)\le K(f).
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:r0-R}
 \frac12\log K(f)\ler_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)\le\log K(f).
\end{equation}
Both constants are best possible; the left-hand constant is sharp in the limiting sense and the right-hand equality occurs, for example, for $\omega(z)=kz$.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Since $0=\omega_f(0)\in E_f$, if $c=c_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)$ and $R=r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:center-to-zero}
 d_{\mathbb D}(0,c)\le R.
\end{equation}
Put
\[
 r_0=\sup_{\zeta\in E_f}d_{\mathbb D}(0,\zeta)=\log K(f).
\]
Since $R$ is the minimum possible covering radius, $R\le r_0$.  Conversely, for every $\zeta\in E_f$,
by the triangle inequality and \eqref{eq:center-to-zero},
\[
 d_{\mathbb D}(0,\zeta)
 \le d_{\mathbb D}(0,c)+d_{\mathbb D}(c,\zeta)
 \le2R.
\]
Thus $r_0\le2R$.  Exponentiating gives \eqref{eq:sqrtK}.

For $\omega(z)=kz$, the image is a hyperbolic ball centered at $0$, so $R=r_0$ and $K_{\mathrm{aff}}=K$.  To see sharpness of the factor $1/2$, fix $R>0$ and choose hyperbolic balls $B_{\mathbb D}(c_j,R)$ with $0$ in their interior and
\[
 d_{\mathbb D}(0,c_j)\longrightarrow R^-\ \text{as }j\to\infty.
\]
Choose conformal mappings \[\omega_j:\mathbb D\to B_{\mathbb D}(c_j,R)\] normalized by $\omega_j(0)=0$, and realize them by Lemma~\ref{lem:realization}.  Then $r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f_j)=R$, whereas
\[
 \log K(f_j)=R+d_{\mathbb D}(0,c_j)\longrightarrow2R,\quad j\to\infty.
\]
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
The inequality \eqref{eq:sqrtK} explains the precise limitation of the usual point normalization.  Eliminating $\omega(0)$ can lose at most a square in the maximal differential distortion relative to the globally optimal affine gauge; in the univalent category, this is a statement about quasiconformal constants, and the loss cannot be improved uniformly.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:canonical-section}
The definition \eqref{eq:Bal-def} is independent of the chosen minimizing affine mapping $A$.  Moreover, for every orientation-preserving real-affine target mapping $B$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Bal-affine-invariant}
 \mathscr B[B\circ f]=\mathscr B[f].
\end{equation}
Thus $\mathscr B$ is a canonical section of the target-affine quotient, normalized by \eqref{eq:Bal-normalization}.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Let $A_1$ and $A_2$ be two minimizing affine mappings.  By Theorem \ref{thm:optimal}, there is a similarity $S(w)=\lambda w+\gamma$ with $\lambda\ne0$, such that
\(
 A_2=S\circ A_1.
\)
Therefore,
\begin{align*}
 \frac{A_2(f(z))-A_2(f(0))}{(A_2\circ f)_z(0)}
 =\frac{\lambda(A_1(f(z))-A_1(f(0)))}
 {\lambda(A_1\circ f)_z(0)}
 =\frac{A_1(f(z))-A_1(f(0))}{(A_1\circ f)_z(0)}.
\end{align*}
This proves well-definedness.                        

Now let $B$ be target-affine.  The affine orbit of $B\circ f$ is exactly the affine orbit of $f$, so the set of balanced representatives is the same modulo similarities.  Applying the normalization \eqref{eq:Bal-normalization} gives the same unique element.  Hence \eqref{eq:Bal-affine-invariant} holds.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:Bal-Koebe}
For every orientation-preserving harmonic mapping $f$ with $\left\lVert \omega_f\right\rVert_\infty<1$ and every $\phi\in\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb D)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Bal-intertwine}
 \mathscr B[f\circ\phi]
 =\mathcal K_\phi(\mathscr B[f]).
\end{equation}
In particular, applying a Koebe transform to a balanced mapping and rebalancing produces exactly the normalized Koebe transform of its canonical affine class.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Let $A$ balance $f$.  Since $\omega_{f\circ\phi}(\mathbb D)=\omega_f(\mathbb D)$, the same affine mapping $A$ balances $f\circ\phi$.  Substituting $A\circ f$ into \eqref{eq:Bal-def} and normalizing at $\phi(0)$ gives \eqref{eq:Bal-intertwine}.  Any target similarity discrepancy disappears by the normalization, as in Theorem~\ref{thm:canonical-section}.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:HD-stable}
For every $D\ge0$, the classes $\mathscr H(D)$ and $\mathscr S(D)$ are invariant under:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item all orientation-preserving real-affine postcompositions;
\item all conformal automorphisms of the source disk;
\item all target similarities and the normalizations used in harmonic Koebe transforms.
\end{enumerate}
Furthermore,
\[
 \mathscr H(0)
 =\{\text{Target-affine images of locally univalent analytic mappings}\},
\]
and similarly in the univalent category.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
The invariance follows from Proposition \ref{prop:full-invariance}, and the zero-level characterization follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:zero-defect}.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:uniform-balanced}
If $f\in\mathscr H(D)$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform-balanced-K}
 K(\mathscr B[f])=K_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)
 \le \exp (J(D)).
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform-balanced-k}
 \left\lVert \omega_{\mathscr B[f]}\right\rVert_\infty
 \le \tanh\frac{J(D)}2.
\end{equation}
The bound is sharp.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
This is Theorem~\ref{thm:affine-jung} together with Corollary~\ref{cor:balanced-k}.  Sharpness follows from the equilateral-triangle construction in Section~\ref{sec:examples}.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
The parameter $D$ measures the oscillation of the complex dilatation rather than its displacement from a chosen origin.  It therefore behaves like a gauge-invariant curvature of the affine orbit: $D=0$ is exactly the affine-analytic locus, while finite $D$ gives a quantitatively controlled departure from that locus.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:radius-Hausdorff}
If $d_H(E,F)\le\varepsilon$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:radius-lipschitz}
 |\operatorname{rad}_{\mathbb D}(E)-\operatorname{rad}_{\mathbb D}(F)|\le\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
For every $p\in\mathbb D$ and every $x\in E$, choose $y\in F$ with $d(x,y)\le\varepsilon$.  Then
\[
 d(p,x)\le d(p,y)+\varepsilon
 \le r_F(p)+\varepsilon.
\]
Hence $r_E(p)\le r_F(p)+\varepsilon$.  Taking infima in $p$ gives
\[
 \operatorname{rad}(E)\le\operatorname{rad}(F)+\varepsilon.
\]
Interchanging $E$ and $F$ proves the claim.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:center-Hausdorff}
Let $c_E,c_F$ and $R_E,R_F$ be the circumcenters and circumradii of compact hyperbolically bounded sets $E,F\subset\mathbb D$.  If $d_H(E,F)\le\varepsilon$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:center-stability}
 d_{\mathbb D}(c_E,c_F)^2
 \le 8R_E\,\varepsilon+8\varepsilon^2.
\end{equation}
The same estimate holds with $R_E$ replaced by $R_F$.  In particular, if $E_n\to E$ in hyperbolic Hausdorff distance, then $c_{E_n}\to c_E$ and $R_{E_n}\to R_E$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
In a CAT$(0)$ space, if $m$ is the midpoint of $c_E$ and an arbitrary point $x$, then for every $y\in E$,
\[
 d(m,y)^2
 \le\frac12d(c_E,y)^2+\frac12d(x,y)^2
 -\frac14d(c_E,x)^2.
\]
Taking the supremum over $y\in E$ gives
\[
 r_E(m)^2
 \le\frac12R_E^2+\frac12r_E(x)^2
 -\frac14d(c_E,x)^2.
\]
Since $c_E$ minimizes the radius, $R_E\le r_E(m)$, and therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:strong-radius}
 d(c_E,x)^2
 \le2\bigl(r_E(x)^2-R_E^2\bigr).
\end{equation}
Take $x=c_F$.  Hausdorff closeness gives
\[
 r_E(c_F)\le R_F+\varepsilon
 \le R_E+2\varepsilon
\]
by Lemma~\ref{lem:radius-Hausdorff}.  Substituting in \eqref{eq:strong-radius}, we have
\begin{align*}
 d(c_E,c_F)^2
 \le2\bigl[(R_E+2\varepsilon)^2-R_E^2\bigr]
 =8R_E\,\varepsilon+8\varepsilon^2.
\end{align*}
The symmetric estimate follows by interchanging $E$ and $F$.  The convergence statement is immediate.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:Hinf-stability}
Let $f_n=h_n+\overline{g_n}$ and $f=h+\overline g$ be orientation-preserving harmonic mappings such that, for some $0\le k<1$,
\[
 \left\lVert \omega_{f_n}\right\rVert_\infty\le k,
 \quad
 \left\lVert \omega_f\right\rVert_\infty\le k,
\]
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Hinf-omega}
 \left\lVert \omega_{f_n}-\omega_f\right\rVert_\infty\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{align}
 r_{\mathrm{aff}}(f_n)&\tor_{\mathrm{aff}}(f),\label{eq:rA-cont}\\
 d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f_n)&\tod_{\mathrm{aff}}(f),\label{eq:dA-cont}\\
 c_{\mathrm{aff}}(f_n)&\toc_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)\ \text{in }d_{\mathbb D},\label{eq:cA-cont}\\
 K_{\mathrm{aff}}(f_n)&\toK_{\mathrm{aff}}(f).
\end{align}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
On the compact Euclidean disk $|z|\le k$, the hyperbolic and Euclidean metrics are bi-Lipschitz equivalent.  Thus \eqref{eq:Hinf-omega} implies that the compact sets
\(
 E_{f_n}=\overline{\omega_{f_n}(\mathbb D)}
\)
converge to $E_f$ in hyperbolic Hausdorff distance.  The conclusions for radius and center follow from Lemmas~\ref{lem:radius-Hausdorff} and \ref{lem:center-Hausdorff}.  Diameter is Lipschitz with respect to Hausdorff distance with constant $2$, and the conclusion for $K_{\mathrm{aff}}$ follows by exponentiation.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:normality}
Fix $D<\infty$.  Let $f_n\in\mathscr S(D)$ and set
\(
 F_n=\mathscr B[f_n].
\)
Then $\{F_n\}$ is a normal family in the topology of locally uniform convergence.  More precisely, with
\[
 k_D=\tanh\frac{J(D)}2<1,
\]
every $F_n=H_n+\overline{G_n}$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:normal-kD}
 \left\lVert G_n'/H_n'\right\rVert_\infty\le k_D,
\end{equation}
and every sequence admits a locally uniformly convergent subsequence whose limit is a normalized orientation-preserving univalent harmonic mapping with quasiconformal constant at most $(1+k_D)/(1-k_D)$.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
The bound \eqref{eq:normal-kD} is Corollary~\ref{cor:uniform-balanced}.  Write
\(
 b_n=G_n'(0),
\ |b_n|\le k_D.
\)
Consider the standard affine normalization
\begin{equation}\label{eq:standard-affine-normalization}
 \widetilde F_n
 =\frac{F_n-\overline{b_n}\,\overline{F_n}}
 {1-|b_n|^2}.
\end{equation}
Then $\widetilde F_n(0)=0$, $(\widetilde F_n)_z(0)=1$, and $(\widetilde F_n)_{\overline z}(0)=0$.  Since affine postcomposition preserves univalence and orientation-preservation, i.e., $\widetilde F_n\in\mathcal S_H^0$.

The standard family $\mathcal S_H^0$ is compact in the topology of locally uniform convergence; see Clunie-Sheil-Small~\cite{ClunieSheilSmall1984} or Duren~\cite{Duren2004}.  Passing to a subsequence, assume
\[
 \widetilde F_n\longrightarrow\widetilde F
\]
locally uniformly and $b_n\to b$ with $|b|\le k_D$.  Solving \eqref{eq:standard-affine-normalization} for $F_n$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:recover-F}
 F_n=\widetilde F_n+\overline{b_n}\,\overline{\widetilde F_n}.
\end{equation}
Hence
\[
 F_n\longrightarrow F
 =\widetilde F+\overline b\,\overline{\widetilde F}
\]
locally uniformly.  By the compactness theorem for $\mathcal S_H^0$, the limit $\widetilde F$ belongs to $\mathcal S_H^0$.  Since $|b|\le k_D<1$, the real-affine mapping $L_b(w)=w+\overline b\,\overline w$ is orientation-preserving, and $F=L_b\circ\widetilde F$ is therefore normalized, orientation-preserving, and univalent.  Local uniform convergence of harmonic mappings implies local uniform convergence of their first derivatives; hence the pointwise bound $|G_n'|\le k_D|H_n'|$ passes to the limit and gives $|G'|\le k_D|H'|$ on $\mathbb D$.  Thus $F$ is a quasiconformal homeomorphism onto its image with constant at most $(1+k_D)/(1-k_D)$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
The limit in Theorem~\ref{thm:normality} need not remain balanced without stronger, global convergence of the dilatations.  Boundary-scale oscillation can disappear under locally uniform convergence.  This is why Proposition~\ref{prop:Hinf-stability} is formulated in the $H^\infty$ topology.  The normality theorem should therefore be read as precompactness of the canonical affine quotient section, not as closedness of the balanced locus in the compact-open topology.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:scaled-SP}
Let $\Omega:\mathbb D\to k\mathbb D$ be analytic with $0<k<1$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:scaled-SP}
 |\Omega'(z)|
 \le
 \frac{k^2-|\Omega(z)|^2}
 {k(1-|z|^2)}.
\end{equation}
Equality at one point occurs if and only if $\Omega/k$ is a disk automorphism.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Applying the Schwarz-Pick lemma to $\psi=\Omega/k$, we obtain
\[
 \frac{|\psi'(z)|}{1-|\psi(z)|^2}
 \le\frac1{1-|z|^2}.
\]
Multiplying by $k$ and simplifying gives \eqref{eq:scaled-SP}.  The equality case follows from the classical equality condition for the Schwarz-Pick lemma.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:Ck-max}
For $0<k<1$, $\Phi_k$ has a unique maximum in $(0,k)$.  If
\begin{equation}\label{eq:xk}
 x_k=\frac{3-k^2-\sqrt{(1-k^2)(9-k^2)}}2,
\end{equation}
then the maximizing point is $t_k=\sqrt{x_k}$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Ck}
 \max_{0\le t\le k}\Phi_k(t)
 =\mathcal C(k)
 :=\frac{\sqrt{x_k}(k^2-x_k)}{k(1-x_k)}
 =\frac{2x_k^{3/2}}{k(1+x_k)}.
\end{equation}
Furthermore,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Ck-small}
 \mathcal C(k)=\frac{2}{3\sqrt3}k^2+O(k^4)
 \quad(k\to0).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Differentiation shows that, after removal of the positive factor $1/k$, the numerator of $\Phi_k'(t)$ is
\[
 k^2+(k^2-3)t^2+t^4.
\]
With $x=t^2$, the critical-point equation is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-poly}
 x^2+(k^2-3)x+k^2=0.
\end{equation}
The smaller root is $x_k$ in \eqref{eq:xk}.  Since $\Phi_k'(0)>0$ and the left derivative at $t=k$ is negative, this root lies in $(0,k^2)$ and is the unique maximizing critical point.

At the critical point, \eqref{eq:critical-poly} is equivalent to
\begin{equation}\label{eq:k2-xrelation}
 k^2=\frac{x(3-x)}{1+x}.
\end{equation}
Thus
\[
 k^2-x=\frac{2x(1-x)}{1+x},
\]
which gives the second expression in \eqref{eq:Ck}.  Finally,
\[
 \sqrt{(1-k^2)(9-k^2)}
 =3-\frac53k^2+O(k^4),
 \quad
 x_k=\frac{k^2}{3}+O(k^4),
\]
and substitution into \eqref{eq:Ck} gives \eqref{eq:Ck-small}.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:sharp-Pgap}
Let $F=H+\overline G$ be an orientation-preserving harmonic mapping in $\mathbb D$ and assume
\[
 k=\left\lVert G'/H'\right\rVert_\infty<1.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sharp-Pgap}
 \left\lVert P_H-P_F\right\rVert\le\mathcal C(k),
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal C$ is given by \eqref{eq:Ck} with $\mathcal C(0)=0$.  The inequality is sharp for every $0<k<1$, even among globally univalent harmonic quasiconformal mappings.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
The estimate is immediate from \eqref{eq:pointwise-C} and Lemma~\ref{lem:Ck-max}. To show sharpness, consider
\(F_k:=f_k\) given by \eqref{63}.
Then $H(z)=z$, $G(z)=kz^2/2$, and $\Omega(z)=kz$.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:realization}, $F_k$ is globally univalent and quasiconformal. Moreover, the dilatation has image \(k\mathbb D\), so that equality holds in the Schwarz-Pick lemma.  For $r=|z|$,
\[
 (1-r^2)|P_H-P_{F_k}|
 =\frac{k^2r(1-r^2)}{1-k^2r^2}
 =\Phi_k(kr).
\]
Choosing $r=\sqrt{x_k}/k\in(0,1)$ attains $\mathcal C(k)$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:C-monotone}
The function $\mathcal C:[0,1)\to[0,1)$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1)$, with
\[
 \mathcal C(0)=0,
 \quad
 \lim_{k\to1^-}\mathcal C(k)=1.
\]
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
For fixed $0<t<k$,
\[
 \Phi_k(t)
 =\frac{t}{1-t^2}\left(k-\frac{t^2}{k}\right)
\]
is strictly increasing in $k$.  If $0<k_1<k_2<1$ and $t_1$ is the unique maximizer for $k_1$, then
\[
 \mathcal C(k_2)\ge \Phi_{k_2}(t_1)
 >\Phi_{k_1}(t_1)=\mathcal C(k_1).
\]
The endpoint limits follow from Lemma~\ref{lem:Ck-max}; in particular, $x_k\to1$ as $k\to1^-$ and the second expression in \eqref{eq:Ck} tends to $1$.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:affine-optimal-Pgap}
Under the preceding assumptions,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:affine-optimal-Pgap}
 \left\lVert P_H-P_f\right\rVert
 =\left\lVert P_H-P_F\right\rVert
 \le\mathcal C(k_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)).
\end{equation}
For every target-affine representative $A\circ f$ with analytic part $H_A$,
\[
 \left\lVert P_{H_A}-P_f\right\rVert
 \le \mathcal C\!\left(\left\lVert \omega_{A\circ f}\right\rVert_\infty\right),
\]
and the parameter on the right is minimized by a balancing mapping.  The bound \eqref{eq:affine-optimal-Pgap} is sharp for every $0<k_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)<1$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
The equality $P_F=P_f$ follows from target-affine invariance of the harmonic pre-Schwarzian.  Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp-Pgap} to $F$ and use \eqref{eq:k-affine-min}.  The second assertion follows from the same universal theorem applied to $A\circ f$, and monotonicity follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:C-monotone}.  Sharpness is realized by the balanced mappings $F_k$ in \eqref{63}.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Let $F=\mathscr B[f]=H+\overline G$ and put $\Omega=G'/H'$ and $k=\|\Omega\|_\infty=k_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)$.  Target-affine invariance of the harmonic pre-Schwarzian gives $P_F=P_f$, hence
\[
 P_H-P_f=P_H-P_F=\frac{\overline\Omega\,\Omega'}{1-|\Omega|^2}.
\]
If $k=0$, then $\Omega\equiv0$ and the assertion is immediate.  Assume $0<k<1$.  Applying Schwarz-Pick lemma to $\Omega/k:\mathbb D\to\mathbb D$ yields
\[
 |\Omega'(z)|\le\frac{k^2-|\Omega(z)|^2}{k(1-|z|^2)}.
\]
Therefore, with $t=|\Omega(z)|$,
\[
 (1-|z|^2)|P_H(z)-P_f(z)|
 \le\frac{t(k^2-t^2)}{k(1-t^2)}=\Phi_k(t).
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:Ck-max}, we get \[\max_{0\le t\le k}\Phi_k(t)=\mathcal C(k)\] with $\mathcal C$ given by \eqref{eq:Ck}; this proves \eqref{eq:intro-ps}.  The expansion \eqref{eq:Ck-asymptotic-intro} is \eqref{eq:Ck-small}.

For sharpness, consider the balanced globally univalent harmonic quasiconformal mapping $F_k = f_k$ given by \eqref{63}, with
\(\Omega(z)=kz\).
Equality holds in the Schwarz-Pick lemma for $\Omega/k = z$, and at $|z|=\sqrt{x_k}/k$, the function $\Phi_k(k|z|)$ equals $\mathcal C(k)$.  Thus equality is attained for every $0<k<1$.

Finally, if $A$ is any orientation-preserving target-affine mapping and $k_A=\|\omega_{A\circ f}\|_\infty$, the same argument gives the universal bound with $\mathcal C(k_A)$.  By Theorem~\ref{thm:intro-optimal}, $k_A$ is minimized exactly by a balancing gauge, and by Propostion~\ref{prop:C-monotone} so is $\mathcal C(k_A)$.  This proves the affine-optimal assertion.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- example-7: body_md -->
Consider \(f_k(z)\) given by \eqref{63}. By our realization lemma, since \(\omega_f(\mathbb D)=k\mathbb D\) is centered at the origin, \(f_k\) is already its own canonical balanced representative, so \(F=B[f_k]=f_k\) and \(k_{\text{aff}}(f_k)=k\). Theorem~\ref{thm:intro-ps} yields \(\|P_H-P_{f_k}\|\le C(k)\). This mapping does not realize equality; hence the inequality is strict. Moreover, for any orientation-preserving real-affine target mapping \(A\), we have \(\|\omega_{A\circ f_k}\|_\infty\ge k\), confirming that balancing minimizes the relevant parameter over the affine orbit.
<!-- end example-7 -->
<!-- example-8: body_md -->
For fixed \(0<k<1\), take an analytic dilatation \(\omega\) whose image set satisfies the three‑point support geometry realizing the extremum of the pre-Schwarzian shadow functional, with parameters governed by the root \(x_k\) from formula \eqref{eq:xk-intro}. Applying our realization lemma and the canonical balancing procedure yields the balanced representative \(F=H+\overline G\). By construction \(\|G'/H'\|_\infty=k_{\text{aff}}(f)=k\) and \(\|P_H-P_F\|=C(k)\), so equality holds in estimate \eqref{eq:intro-ps}. As \(k\to 0\), the shadow magnitude behaves as \(\frac{2}{3\sqrt 3}k^2+O(k^4)\), consistent with the asymptotic expansion \eqref{eq:Ck-asymptotic-intro}. This example demonstrates sharpness for every admissible \(k\).
<!-- end example-8 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:Pnorm-comparison}
If $F=H+\overline G$ is as in Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp-Pgap}, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Pnorm-comparison}
 \bigl|\left\lVert P_H\right\rVert-\left\lVert P_F\right\rVert\bigr|
 \le\mathcal C(k).
\end{equation}
In particular,
\[
 \bigl|\left\lVert P_H\right\rVert-\left\lVert P_F\right\rVert\bigr|
 \le\frac{2}{3\sqrt3}k^2+O(k^4)
 \quad(k\to0).
\]
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Applying the triangle inequality in the weighted supremum norm and invoking Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp-Pgap}, we
get the desired assertion.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:a2-shadow}
Suppose that
\(
 F(0)=0,\ H'(0)=1,
\)
and write
\[
 H(z)=z+a_2z^2+a_3z^3+\cdots.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:a2-shadow}
 \left|2a_2-P_F(0)\right|
 \le\mathcal C(k).
\end{equation}
The constant is sharp, even in the class of balanced normalized globally univalent harmonic quasiconformal mappings.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Since $P_H(0)=H''(0)/H'(0)=2a_2$, the inequality is the pointwise consequence of Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp-Pgap}. For sharpness, let $t_k=\sqrt{x_k}$ and choose $a=t_k/k\in(0,1)$.  Put
\[
 \Omega_{k,a}(z)
 =k\frac{z+a}{1+az}.
\]
Then $\Omega_{k,a}/k$ is a disk automorphism, $\Omega_{k,a}(\mathbb D)=k\mathbb D$, and $|\Omega_{k,a}(0)|=t_k$.  Define
\[
 G_{k,a}(z)=\int_0^z\Omega_{k,a}(\zeta)\,d\zeta,
 \quad
 F_{k,a}(z)=z+\overline{G_{k,a}(z)}.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:realization}, $F_{k,a}$ is globally univalent and quasiconformal; it is balanced because its dilatation image is $k\mathbb D$, and it satisfies $F_{k,a}(0)=0$, $H'(0)=1$.  Equality holds in Lemma~\ref{lem:scaled-SP} at $0$, while $|\Omega_{k,a}(0)|=t_k$ is the maximizing value in Lemma~\ref{lem:Ck-max}.  Hence
\[
 |2a_2-P_{F_{k,a}}(0)|=\mathcal C(k).
\]
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rem:quadratic-significance}
The quadratic small-$k$ behavior is a consequence of using the full bound $\Omega(\mathbb D)\subset k\mathbb D$ in Schwarz-Pick lemma; it is available in every fixed affine gauge.  The genuinely affine statement is that balancing replaces the gauge-dependent number $\left\lVert \omega_{A\circ f}\right\rVert_\infty$ by its minimum $k_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)$.  Thus balancing gives the strongest member of the sharp family of estimates \eqref{eq:sharp-Pgap}, rather than changing the order of the Schwarz-Pick estimate itself.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:orders}
Under \eqref{eq:family-k0}, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:order-comparison}
 \left|
 \alpha_\flat(\mathcal F)-\sigma_\flat(\mathcal F)
 \right|
 \le\frac12\mathcal C(k_0).
\end{equation}
If the family is contained in $\mathcal S^{\flat}(D)$, one may take
\begin{equation}\label{eq:k0-D}
 k_0=\tanh\frac{J(D)}2.
\end{equation}
Consequently, for small $D$ the difference between the two orders is quadratic in the affine defect.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
For each $F=H+\overline G$ in the balanced family, Corollary~\ref{cor:a2-shadow} gives
\[
 |2a_2(F)-P_F(0)|\le\mathcal C(k_0),
\]
because $\mathcal C$ is increasing by Proposition~\ref{prop:C-monotone}.  Hence
\[
 2|a_2(F)|\le|P_F(0)|+\mathcal C(k_0)
\]
and
\[
 |P_F(0)|\le2|a_2(F)|+\mathcal C(k_0).
\]
Taking suprema yields \eqref{eq:order-comparison}.  The choice \eqref{eq:k0-D} follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:uniform-balanced}.  Finally, \[J(D)=\frac{D}{\sqrt3}+O(D^3)\] and \[k_0=\frac{J(D)}{2}+O(D^3),\] while \[\mathcal C(k_0)=O(k_0^2)=O(D^2).\]
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:Pnorm-order}
Let $\mathcal F^{\flat}$ be balanced-linearly invariant and let $\sigma_\flat=\sigma_\flat(\mathcal F)<\infty$.  Then every $F\in\mathcal F^{\flat}$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Pnorm-sigma}
 \left\lVert P_F\right\rVert\le2(\sigma_\flat+1).
\end{equation}
Consequently, under \eqref{eq:family-k0},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Pnorm-alpha}
 \left\lVert P_F\right\rVert
 \le2\alpha_\flat(\mathcal F)
 +\mathcal C(k_0)+2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Fix $a\in\mathbb D$.  Apply the normalized Koebe transform corresponding to $\phi_a$, followed by balancing.  The resulting mapping belongs to $\mathcal F^{\flat}$, and target-affine transformations do not change the pre-Schwarzian.  Hence the chain rule at $0$ gives
\[
 \left|(1-|a|^2)P_F(a)-2\overline a\right|
 \le2\sigma_\flat.
\]
Therefore,
\[
 (1-|a|^2)|P_F(a)|
 \le2\sigma_\flat+2|a|
 \le2(\sigma_\flat+1).
\]
Taking the supremum over $a$ proves \eqref{eq:Pnorm-sigma}.  The estimate \eqref{eq:Pnorm-alpha} follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:orders}.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:second-order}
Let $f$ be an orientation-preserving harmonic mapping with $\left\lVert \omega_f\right\rVert_\infty<1$ and $d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)=D$, and let
\(
 F=\mathscr B[f]=H+\overline G.
\)
As $D\to0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:second-order}
 \left\lVert P_H-P_F\right\rVert
 \le\frac{D^2}{18\sqrt3}+O(D^4).
\end{equation}
Since $P_F=P_f$ by target-affine invariance,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:second-order-original}
 \left\lVert P_H-P_f\right\rVert
 \le\frac{D^2}{18\sqrt3}+O(D^4).
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
By \eqref{eq:Ck-small}, \eqref{eq:k-D-small}, and Theorem~\ref{thm:sharp-Pgap}, the leading coefficient is
\[
 \frac{2}{3\sqrt3}\left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt3}\right)^2
 =\frac1{18\sqrt3}.
\]
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
An orientation-preserving harmonic mapping of uniformly bounded differential distortion is of \emph{two-support type} if the circumcenter of $E_f$ is determined by two contact points; it is of \emph{three-support type} if no pair of contact points determines the circumcenter.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:quant-affine-analytic}
Let $f$ be an orientation-preserving harmonic mapping with $\left\lVert \omega_f\right\rVert_\infty<1$ and $d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)=D$.  Then there exists an orientation-preserving target-affine mapping $A$ such that $F=A\circ f=H+\overline G$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quant-omega}
 \left\lVert G'/H'\right\rVert_\infty
 \le\tanh\left[
 \frac12\operatorname{arcsinh}\!\left(
 \frac{2}{\sqrt3}\sinh\frac D2
 \right)
 \right].
\end{equation}
The right-hand side is sharp.  In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quant-omega-small}
 \left\lVert G'/H'\right\rVert_\infty
 \le\frac{D}{2\sqrt3}+O(D^3).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
Take $A$ to be a balancing affine mapping and use Theorem \ref{thm:affine-jung} and Corollary~\ref{cor:balanced-k}.  Sharpness follows from the equilateral triangle construction.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- problem-1: body_md -->
\label{prob:balanced-order}
Determine the exact balanced coefficient order of the affine quotient of $\mathcal S_H$ under a fixed affine diameter constraint:
\[
 \alpha_\flat(D)
 =\sup\{|a_2(\mathscr B[f])|:f\in\mathcal S_H,\ d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)\le D\}.
\]
Find the extremal mappings and determine whether they are generated by a hyperbolically symmetric dilatation domain.
<!-- end problem-1 -->
<!-- problem-2: body_md -->
\label{prob:Schwarzian-shadow}
Find the sharp function $\mathcal S(k,M)$ such that every balanced harmonic mapping $f=H+\overline G$ with $k_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)\le k$ and $\left\lVert P_f\right\rVert\le M$ satisfies
\(
 \left\lVert S_H-S_f\right\rVert\le\mathcal S(k,M).
\)
Determine the optimal small-$k$ asymptotics.
<!-- end problem-2 -->
<!-- problem-3: body_md -->
\label{prob:higher-moments}
Develop affine-invariant distortion theory based on other hyperbolic convex-geometric functionals of $E_f$, such as width, inradius, area of $\operatorname{hconv}E_f$, or conformal capacity.  Determine which of these control geometric properties of $f(\mathbb D)$ more efficiently than $r_{\mathrm{aff}}$ and $d_{\mathrm{aff}}$ alone.
<!-- end problem-3 -->
<!-- problem-4: body_md -->
\label{prob:boundary}
Let $f:\mathbb D\to\Omega$ be a harmonic quasiconformal homeomorphism onto a smooth or chord-arc Jordan domain.  Determine whether boundary Lipschitz, co-Lipschitz, or H\"older constants can be estimated naturally in terms of $K_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)$ or $d_{\mathrm{aff}}(f)$ rather than the gauge-dependent $K(f)$.
<!-- end problem-4 -->
<!-- problem-5: body_md -->
\label{prob:higher-dim}
Find an analogue of affine balancing for harmonic quasiconformal mappings in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge3$.  In the plane, the space of linear conformal structures is the hyperbolic disk and the complex dilatation provides a holomorphic coordinate.  In higher dimensions, the space of oriented linear conformal structures, after quotienting by scale, may be identified with the symmetric space
\(
 \mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb R)/\mathrm{SO}(n),
\)
and the local distortion tensor replaces $\omega$.  Is the optimal target-affine distortion determined by a circumcenter problem in this nonpositively curved symmetric space, and under what hypotheses does this recover the quasiconformal constant of a harmonic homeomorphism?
<!-- end problem-5 -->
